claim: CEP89 is important for preciliary vesicle recruitment but not for other steps of cilium formation.
source: In an accompanying paper, we show that the distal appendage protein, CEP89, is important for the preciliary vesicle recruitment, but not for other steps of cilium formation (Kanie et al., 2025).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to an accompanying paper (Kanie et al., 2025).

claim: CEP89 lacks a membrane-binding motif.
source: The lack of a membrane-binding motif in CEP89 suggests that it may indirectly recruit preciliary vesicles via another binding partner.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the protein sequence/structure of CEP89.

claim: NCS1 is a stoichiometric interactor of CEP89.
source: Here, we identify Neuronal Calcium Sensor-1 (NCS1) as a stoichiometric interactor of CEP89.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from tandem affinity purification and mass spectrometry shown in Figure 1.

claim: NCS1 localizes to the position between CEP89 and the centriole-associated vesicle marker, RAB34, at the distal appendage.
source: NCS1 localizes to the position between CEP89 and the centriole-associated vesicle marker, RAB34, at the distal appendage.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2.

claim: NCS1 localization at the distal appendage is completely abolished in CEP89 knockouts.
source: This localization was completely abolished in CEP89 knockouts, suggesting that CEP89 recruits NCS1 to the distal appendage.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2L.

claim: CEP89 recruits NCS1 to the distal appendage.
source: This localization was completely abolished in CEP89 knockouts, suggesting that CEP89 recruits NCS1 to the distal appendage.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that NCS1 localization is lost in CEP89 knockouts.

claim: Preciliary vesicle recruitment is perturbed in NCS1 knockout cells.
source: Similar to CEP89 knockouts, preciliary vesicle recruitment as well as subsequent cilium formation was perturbed in NCS1 knockout cells.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C-E.

claim: Cilium formation is perturbed in NCS1 knockout cells.
source: Similar to CEP89 knockouts, preciliary vesicle recruitment as well as subsequent cilium formation was perturbed in NCS1 knockout cells.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A-B.

claim: The ability of NCS1 to recruit the preciliary vesicle is dependent on its myristoylation motif.
source: The ability of NCS1 to recruit the preciliary vesicle is dependent on its myristoylation motif and NCS1 knockout cells expressing a myristoylation defective mutant failed to rescue the vesicle recruitment defect despite localizing properly to the centriole.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5.

claim: NCS1 knockout cells expressing a myristoylation defective mutant fail to rescue the vesicle recruitment defect despite localizing properly to the centriole.
source: The ability of NCS1 to recruit the preciliary vesicle is dependent on its myristoylation motif and NCS1 knockout cells expressing a myristoylation defective mutant failed to rescue the vesicle recruitment defect despite localizing properly to the centriole.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C-F.

claim: The primary cilium is a microtubule-based organelle that cycles through assembly and disassembly.
source: The primary cilium is a microtubule-based organelle that cycles through assembly and disassembly.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about primary cilia.

claim: In many cell types, formation of the cilium is initiated by recruitment of preciliary vesicles to the distal appendage of the mother centriole.
source: In many cell types, formation of the cilium is initiated by recruitment of preciliary vesicles to the distal appendage of the mother centriole.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about cilium formation pathways.

claim: The distal appendage mechanism that directly captures preciliary vesicles has not been identified prior to this study.
source: However, the distal appendage mechanism that directly captures preciliary vesicles is yet to be identified.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of knowledge in the field prior to this work.

claim: The primary cilium consists of the microtubule-based axoneme surrounded by the ciliary membrane.
source: The primary cilium is an organelle that consists of the microtubule-based axoneme surrounded by the ciliary membrane, which accumulates specific membrane proteins (e.g., G-protein-coupled receptors) to serve as a sensor for extracellular environmental cues (Reiter and Leroux, 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Reiter and Leroux, 2017.

claim: The ciliary membrane accumulates specific membrane proteins (e.g., G-protein-coupled receptors) to serve as a sensor for extracellular environmental cues.
source: The primary cilium is an organelle that consists of the microtubule-based axoneme surrounded by the ciliary membrane, which accumulates specific membrane proteins (e.g., G-protein-coupled receptors) to serve as a sensor for extracellular environmental cues (Reiter and Leroux, 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Reiter and Leroux, 2017.

claim: The cilium extends from the mother centriole.
source: The cilium extends from the mother centriole, and cycles assembly and disassembly, as the cell needs to disassemble the cilium prior to mitosis (Vorobjev and Chentsov Yu, 1982) to allow the centrosome to function within the spindle pole during mitosis.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge supported by citation.

claim: The cell needs to disassemble the cilium prior to mitosis to allow the centrosome to function within the spindle pole during mitosis.
source: The cilium extends from the mother centriole, and cycles assembly and disassembly, as the cell needs to disassemble the cilium prior to mitosis (Vorobjev and Chentsov Yu, 1982) to allow the centrosome to function within the spindle pole during mitosis.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Vorobjev and Chentsov Yu, 1982.

claim: The process of ciliary formation was first described by Sorokin in 1962 and 1968.
source: The process of ciliary formation, described first by Sorokin, 1962; Sorokin, 1968 has been classified into the extra- and intracellular pathways (Molla-Herman et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Sorokin, 1962 and Sorokin, 1968.

claim: Ciliary formation has been classified into the extra- and intracellular pathways.
source: The process of ciliary formation, described first by Sorokin, 1962; Sorokin, 1968 has been classified into the extra- and intracellular pathways (Molla-Herman et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Molla-Herman et al., 2010.

claim: In the extracellular pathway, the mother centriole is believed to first dock to the plasma membrane before the extension of the axonemal microtubule as well as ciliary membrane.
source: In the extracellular pathway used, for example, by Mardin–Darby canine kidney cells, the mother centriole is believed to first dock to the plasma membrane before the extension of the axonemal microtubule as well as ciliary membrane (Jewett et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Jewett et al., 2021.

claim: Mardin-Darby canine kidney cells use the extracellular pathway for cilium formation.
source: In the extracellular pathway used, for example, by Mardin–Darby canine kidney cells, the mother centriole is believed to first dock to the plasma membrane before the extension of the axonemal microtubule as well as ciliary membrane (Jewett et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Jewett et al., 2021.

claim: In the intracellular pathway, the first step of cilium formation is attachment of small vesicles (preciliary vesicles) to the distal end of the mother centriole.
source: In the intracellular pathway used, for example, by retinal pigment epithelia (RPE) cells (Molla-Herman et al., 2010) and fibroblasts (Sorokin, 1962; Molla-Herman et al., 2010), the first step of cilium formation is attachment of the small vesicles, or so-called preciliary vesicles (Lu et al., 2015), to the distal end of the mother centriole (Sorokin, 1962), or more specifically to the distal appendage (Schmidt et al., 2012; Sillibourne et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Retinal pigment epithelia (RPE) cells use the intracellular pathway for cilium formation.
source: In the intracellular pathway used, for example, by retinal pigment epithelia (RPE) cells (Molla-Herman et al., 2010) and fibroblasts (Sorokin, 1962; Molla-Herman et al., 2010), the first step of cilium formation is attachment of the small vesicles, or so-called preciliary vesicles (Lu et al., 2015), to the distal end of the mother centriole (Sorokin, 1962), or more specifically to the distal appendage (Schmidt et al., 2012; Sillibourne et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Molla-Herman et al., 2010.

claim: Fibroblasts use the intracellular pathway for cilium formation.
source: In the intracellular pathway used, for example, by retinal pigment epithelia (RPE) cells (Molla-Herman et al., 2010) and fibroblasts (Sorokin, 1962; Molla-Herman et al., 2010), the first step of cilium formation is attachment of the small vesicles, or so-called preciliary vesicles (Lu et al., 2015), to the distal end of the mother centriole (Sorokin, 1962), or more specifically to the distal appendage (Schmidt et al., 2012; Sillibourne et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Sorokin, 1962 and Molla-Herman et al., 2010.

claim: Preciliary vesicles attach more specifically to the distal appendage of the mother centriole.
source: In the intracellular pathway used, for example, by retinal pigment epithelia (RPE) cells (Molla-Herman et al., 2010) and fibroblasts (Sorokin, 1962; Molla-Herman et al., 2010), the first step of cilium formation is attachment of the small vesicles, or so-called preciliary vesicles (Lu et al., 2015), to the distal end of the mother centriole (Sorokin, 1962), or more specifically to the distal appendage (Schmidt et al., 2012; Sillibourne et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Schmidt et al., 2012 and Sillibourne et al., 2013.

claim: The distal appendage is a ninefold blade-like structure attached to the distal end of the mother centriole.
source: The distal appendage is a ninefold blade-like structure attached to the distal end of the mother centriole (Anderson, 1972; Bowler et al., 2019; Paintrand et al., 1992).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Anderson, 1972; Bowler et al., 2019; and Paintrand et al., 1992.

claim: Preciliary vesicle recruitment is followed by the fusion of the small vesicles to form a large ciliary vesicle.
source: The preciliary vesicle recruitment is followed by the fusion of the small vesicles to form a large ciliary vesicle (Lu et al., 2015), removal of CP110 (Lu et al., 2015), which is believed to cap the distal end of the mother centriole (Spektor et al., 2007), and subsequent axonemal extension, which is mediated at least partially by intraflagellar transport (IFT) (Craft et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Lu et al., 2015.

claim: CP110 removal follows preciliary vesicle recruitment and fusion.
source: The preciliary vesicle recruitment is followed by the fusion of the small vesicles to form a large ciliary vesicle (Lu et al., 2015), removal of CP110 (Lu et al., 2015), which is believed to cap the distal end of the mother centriole (Spektor et al., 2007), and subsequent axonemal extension, which is mediated at least partially by intraflagellar transport (IFT) (Craft et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Lu et al., 2015.

claim: CP110 is believed to cap the distal end of the mother centriole.
source: The preciliary vesicle recruitment is followed by the fusion of the small vesicles to form a large ciliary vesicle (Lu et al., 2015), removal of CP110 (Lu et al., 2015), which is believed to cap the distal end of the mother centriole (Spektor et al., 2007), and subsequent axonemal extension, which is mediated at least partially by intraflagellar transport (IFT) (Craft et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Spektor et al., 2007.

claim: Axonemal extension is mediated at least partially by intraflagellar transport (IFT).
source: The preciliary vesicle recruitment is followed by the fusion of the small vesicles to form a large ciliary vesicle (Lu et al., 2015), removal of CP110 (Lu et al., 2015), which is believed to cap the distal end of the mother centriole (Spektor et al., 2007), and subsequent axonemal extension, which is mediated at least partially by intraflagellar transport (IFT) (Craft et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Craft et al., 2015.

claim: The distal appendage is indispensable for all steps of cilium formation including preciliary vesicle recruitment, vesicle fusion, CP110 removal, and axonemal extension.
source: While the distal appendage is indispensable for all those steps, how exactly the distal appendage controls these multiple processes is largely unknown.
evidence: This is a statement about established knowledge in the field.

claim: How exactly the distal appendage controls multiple processes of cilium formation is largely unknown.
source: While the distal appendage is indispensable for all those steps, how exactly the distal appendage controls these multiple processes is largely unknown.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of knowledge in the field.

claim: CEP89 is important for preciliary vesicle recruitment but not for other processes organizing cilium formation.
source: In an accompanying paper, we comprehensively analyzed all known distal appendage proteins to date and revealed that the Centrosomal Protein 89 (CEP89) is important for preciliary vesicle recruitment, but not for other processes organizing cilium formation (Kanie et al., 2025).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to an accompanying paper (Kanie et al., 2025).

claim: An interacting partner of CEP89 may bind to preciliary vesicle directly.
source: Since CEP89 lacks apparent lipid-binding motifs, we hypothesized that an interacting partner of CEP89 may bind to preciliary vesicle directly.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on inference from the lack of lipid-binding motifs in CEP89.

claim: Tandem affinity purification and mass spectrometry (TAP-MS) identified NCS1 and CEP15 as stoichiometric interactors of CEP89.
source: This analysis identified two stoichiometric interactors, Neuronal Calcium Sensor-1 (NCS1) and CEP15, consistent with the previous high-throughput proteome analyses, which identified both proteins as either CEP89 interactors (Huttlin et al., 2021) or neighbors (Gupta et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A-B and is consistent with previous studies cited.

claim: Previous high-throughput proteome analyses identified NCS1 and CEP15 as either CEP89 interactors or neighbors.
source: This analysis identified two stoichiometric interactors, Neuronal Calcium Sensor-1 (NCS1) and CEP15, consistent with the previous high-throughput proteome analyses, which identified both proteins as either CEP89 interactors (Huttlin et al., 2021) or neighbors (Gupta et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Huttlin et al., 2021 and Gupta et al., 2015.

claim: CEP15 was previously named as C3ORF14.
source: CEP15 was previously named as C3ORF14, and we renamed it to CEP15 to reflect its function.
evidence: This is a statement about nomenclature.

claim: Endogenous NCS1 strongly co-immunoprecipitated with endogenous CEP89.
source: Consistent with the TAP-MS data, endogenous NCS1 strongly co-immunoprecipitated with endogenous CEP89 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: NCS1 is a member of NCS family proteins characterized as containing calcium-binding EF-hand motifs and a myristoylation signal for N-terminal addition of myristate.
source: NCS1 is a member of NCS family proteins, which are characterized as containing calcium-binding EF-hand motifs as well as a myristoylation signal for N-terminal addition of myristate (Burgoyne and Weiss, 2001).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Burgoyne and Weiss, 2001.

claim: NCS1 was first identified as Frequenin in Drosophila, a protein that can facilitate neurotransmitter release in neuromuscular junction.
source: NCS1 was first identified as Frequenin in Drosophila, a protein that can facilitate neurotransmitter release in neuromuscular junction (Pongs et al., 1993).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Pongs et al., 1993.

claim: How exactly NCS-1 regulates neuronal function is still not well understood.
source: However, how exactly NCS-1 regulates neuronal function is still not well understood.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of knowledge in the field.

claim: NCS-1 is expressed ubiquitously in various tissues.
source: As described later in this paper, NCS-1 is expressed ubiquitously in various tissues, consistent with the previous report (Gierke et al., 2004).
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented later in the paper and citation to Gierke et al., 2004.

claim: Previous studies reported roles for NCS1 in cardiomyocytes and adipocytes.
source: While previous studies reported the roles for NCS1 in cardiomyocytes (Nakamura et al., 2011) and adipocytes (Ratai et al., 2019), the function of NCS1 in non-neuronal cells remain enigmatic.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Nakamura et al., 2011 and Ratai et al., 2019.

claim: The function of NCS1 in non-neuronal cells remains enigmatic.
source: While previous studies reported the roles for NCS1 in cardiomyocytes (Nakamura et al., 2011) and adipocytes (Ratai et al., 2019), the function of NCS1 in non-neuronal cells remain enigmatic.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of knowledge in the field.

claim: A centrosomal role of NCS1 has never been described prior to this study.
source: A centrosomal role of NCS1 has never been described.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of knowledge in the field prior to this work.

claim: CEP89 binding to NCS1 requires the N-terminal region (1–343 a.a.) of CEP89.
source: CEP89 binding to NCS1 required the N-terminal region (1–343 a.a.) (Figure 1C, D) in agreement with the structural model of NCS1-CEP89 predicted using Alphafold2 showing that the very N-terminal helix of CEP89 interacts with NCS1 (Figure 2O).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C-D and structural modeling shown in Figure 2O.

claim: The structural model of NCS1-CEP89 predicted using Alphafold2 shows that the very N-terminal helix of CEP89 interacts with NCS1.
source: CEP89 binding to NCS1 required the N-terminal region (1–343 a.a.) (Figure 1C, D) in agreement with the structural model of NCS1-CEP89 predicted using Alphafold2 showing that the very N-terminal helix of CEP89 interacts with NCS1 (Figure 2O).
evidence: The claim is supported by structural modeling data shown in Figure 2O.

claim: The C-terminal portion of CEP89 (344–783 a.a.) is required for its centrosomal localization.
source: The C-terminal portion of CEP89 (344–783 a.a.) is required for its centrosomal localization (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B), consistent with a previous report (Sillibourne et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B and citation to Sillibourne et al., 2013.

claim: HA-tagged CEP89 directly binds to MYC-tagged CEP15 and NCS1 in an in vitro binding assay.
source: An in vitro binding assay using in vitro translated proteins revealed that HA-tagged CEP89 directly binds to MYC-tagged CEP15 and NCS1 (Figure 1E), whereas HA-CEP15 did not bind to NCS1 (Figure 1F).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: HA-CEP15 does not bind to NCS1 in an in vitro binding assay.
source: An in vitro binding assay using in vitro translated proteins revealed that HA-tagged CEP89 directly binds to MYC-tagged CEP15 and NCS1 (Figure 1E), whereas HA-CEP15 did not bind to NCS1 (Figure 1F).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: CEP89 serves to bridge NCS1 and CEP15.
source: Thus, CEP89 serves to bridge NCS1 and CEP15 (Figure 1G).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the binding data showing CEP89 binds both NCS1 and CEP15, but CEP15 does not bind NCS1.

claim: NCS1 localizes to the mother centriole when observed via wide-field microscopy.
source: When observed via a wide-field microscopy, NCS1 localized to the mother centriole, marked by CEP170 (Figure 2A).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: NCS1 shows some cytoplasmic staining in addition to centriolar localization.
source: When observed via a wide-field microscopy, NCS1 localized to the mother centriole, marked by CEP170 (Figure 2A). Some cytoplasmic staining was also observed.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Both centriolar and cytoplasmic NCS1 staining is highly specific as the signal was strongly reduced in NCS1 knockout cells.
source: Both centriolar and cytoplasmic staining was highly specific as the signal was strongly reduced in NCS1 knockout cells (Figure 2A).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2A comparing control and NCS1 knockout cells.

claim: C-terminally EYFP-tagged NCS1 constitutively localizes to membranous compartments according to a previous study.
source: The cytoplasmic localization of NCS1 is inconsistent with a previous study, where C-terminally Enhanced Yellow Fluorescent Protein (EYFP)-tagged NCS1 constitutively localized to membranous compartments (O'Callaghan et al., 2002).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to O'Callaghan et al., 2002.

claim: N-terminally LAP-tagged wild-type NCS1 localizes to mother centriole as well as cytoplasm, similar to endogenous NCS1.
source: N-terminally LAP (EGFP and S)-tagged wild-type or G2A mutant of NCS1 localized to mother centriole as well as cytoplasm, similar to endogenous NCS1 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A, B).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: N-terminally LAP-tagged G2A mutant of NCS1 localizes to mother centriole as well as cytoplasm, similar to endogenous NCS1.
source: N-terminally LAP (EGFP and S)-tagged wild-type or G2A mutant of NCS1 localized to mother centriole as well as cytoplasm, similar to endogenous NCS1 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A, B).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: C-terminally LAP-tagged wild-type NCS1 localizes to membrane compartments, such as plasma membrane and endoplasmic reticulum.
source: Consistent with the previous paper (O'Callaghan et al., 2002), C-terminally LAP-tagged wild-type NCS1 localized to membrane compartments, such as plasma membrane and endoplasmic reticulum, whereas the myristoylation defective mutant (G2A) diffusely localized to cytoplasm (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C, D).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C and citation to O'Callaghan et al., 2002.

claim: C-terminally LAP-tagged myristoylation defective mutant (G2A) of NCS1 diffusely localizes to cytoplasm.
source: Consistent with the previous paper (O'Callaghan et al., 2002), C-terminally LAP-tagged wild-type NCS1 localized to membrane compartments, such as plasma membrane and endoplasmic reticulum, whereas the myristoylation defective mutant (G2A) diffusely localized to cytoplasm (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C, D).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1D.

claim: C-terminal tagging of NCS1 changes its localization potentially via exposing the myristoylation motif of NCS1.
source: This result suggests that C-terminal tagging of NCS1 changes its localization potentially via exposing the myristoylation motif of NCS1, and endogenous NCS1 may sequester its myristoylation motif to allow localization to cytoplasm.
evidence: This is inferred from the difference in localization between N-terminally and C-terminally tagged NCS1.

claim: Endogenous NCS1 may sequester its myristoylation motif to allow localization to cytoplasm.
source: This result suggests that C-terminal tagging of NCS1 changes its localization potentially via exposing the myristoylation motif of NCS1, and endogenous NCS1 may sequester its myristoylation motif to allow localization to cytoplasm.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning based on the observed localization patterns.

claim: C-terminally LAP-tagged CEP15 localizes to the location between acetylated tubulin (a cilium marker) and Pericentrin (a centrosome marker), suggesting it localizes specifically to the mother centriole.
source: Similar to NCS1, C-terminally LAP-tagged CEP15 localized to the location between acetylated tubulin, a cilium marker, and Pericentrin, a centrosome marker, suggesting that it also localizes specifically to the mother centriole (Figure 2B).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: NCS1 localization to the mother centriole is enhanced upon serum deprivation.
source: NCS1 localization to the mother centriole was enhanced upon serum deprivation (Figure 2C), a condition that induces cilium formation in RPE cells, much like several other distal appendage proteins (see Figure 1D of Kanie et al., 2025).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Serum deprivation induces cilium formation in RPE cells.
source: NCS1 localization to the mother centriole was enhanced upon serum deprivation (Figure 2C), a condition that induces cilium formation in RPE cells, much like several other distal appendage proteins (see Figure 1D of Kanie et al., 2025).
evidence: This is established knowledge about RPE cell behavior.

claim: C-terminally LAP-tagged CEP15 localizes to a position slightly distal to the distal appendage protein, CEP164, in side view when observed via 3D-structured illumination microscopy.
source: When observed via 3D-structured illumination microscopy with a resolution twice as high as a diffraction limited microscopy (Wu and Shroff, 2018), C-terminally LAP (EGFP-S)-tagged CEP15 localized to a position slightly distal to the distal appendage protein, CEP164, in side view (Figure 2D).
evidence: The claim is supported by super-resolution microscopy data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: LAP-CEP15 forms a ring-like structure that is slightly smaller than the CEP164 ring when viewed from the top (axial view) of the mother centriole.
source: When top (or axial) view of the mother centriole was visualized, LAP-CEP15 formed a ring-like structure that is slightly smaller than the CEP164 ring (Figure 2E), which mirrors the ninefold symmetrical structure of the distal appendage (Paintrand et al., 1992).
evidence: The claim is supported by super-resolution microscopy data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: NCS1 localizes slightly distal to CEP164.
source: Similarly, NCS1 localized slightly distal to CEP164 (Figure 2F) as well as the binding partner, CEP89 (Figure 2G), and slightly proximal to the centriole-associated vesicle marker, RAB34 (Stuck et al., 2021; Kanie et al., 2025; Figure 2H).
evidence: The claim is supported by super-resolution microscopy data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: NCS1 localizes slightly distal to CEP89.
source: Similarly, NCS1 localized slightly distal to CEP164 (Figure 2F) as well as the binding partner, CEP89 (Figure 2G), and slightly proximal to the centriole-associated vesicle marker, RAB34 (Stuck et al., 2021; Kanie et al., 2025; Figure 2H).
evidence: The claim is supported by super-resolution microscopy data shown in Figure 2G.

claim: NCS1 localizes slightly proximal to the centriole-associated vesicle marker, RAB34.
source: Similarly, NCS1 localized slightly distal to CEP164 (Figure 2F) as well as the binding partner, CEP89 (Figure 2G), and slightly proximal to the centriole-associated vesicle marker, RAB34 (Stuck et al., 2021; Kanie et al., 2025; Figure 2H).
evidence: The claim is supported by super-resolution microscopy data shown in Figure 2H and citations.

claim: NCS1 forms a slightly smaller ring than CEP164 when viewed from the top of the mother centriole.
source: Like CEP15, NCS1 formed a slightly smaller ring than CEP164 (Figure 2I).
evidence: The claim is supported by super-resolution microscopy data shown in Figure 2I.

claim: The ring diameter of NCS1 is 319.5 ± 7.7 nm (n = 13, average ± SEM).
source: Consistent with this, the ring diameter of NCS1 and CEP15 was 319.5 ± 7.7 nm (n = 13, average ± SEM) and 348.8 ± 8.0 nm (n = 16, average ± SEM), respectively (see Figure 1C of Kanie et al., 2025).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantification data referenced in an accompanying paper.

claim: The ring diameter of CEP15 is 348.8 ± 8.0 nm (n = 16, average ± SEM).
source: Consistent with this, the ring diameter of NCS1 and CEP15 was 319.5 ± 7.7 nm (n = 13, average ± SEM) and 348.8 ± 8.0 nm (n = 16, average ± SEM), respectively (see Figure 1C of Kanie et al., 2025).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantification data referenced in an accompanying paper.

claim: Both CEP15 and NCS1 localize to the region close to subdistal appendage in some but not all centrioles.
source: It is notable that both CEP15 and NCS1 also localized to the region close to subdistal appendage in some but not all centrioles (Figure 2D, F), consistent with what was observed for CEP89 localization (Chong et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 2D and 2F, and citation to Chong et al., 2020.

claim: CEP15 was previously classified as a subdistal appendage protein.
source: This near subdistal appendage localization explains why CEP15 was previously classified as a subdistal appendage protein (Gupta et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Gupta et al., 2015.

claim: Centriolar localization of CEP89 is not affected by depletion of either NCS1 or CEP15.
source: Centriolar localization of CEP89 was not affected by depletion of either NCS1 nor CEP15 (Figure 2K and Figure 2—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2K and Figure 2—figure supplement 2A.

claim: NCS1 fails to localize to the mother centriole in CEP89 knockout cells.
source: NCS1 failed to localize to the mother centriole without altering its cytoplasmic localization in CEP89 knockout cells but not in CEP15 knockout cells (Figure 2L and Figure 2—figure supplement 2B), indicating that CEP89 recruits NCS1 to the distal appendage.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2L and Figure 2—figure supplement 2B.

claim: NCS1 localizes to the mother centriole in CEP15 knockout cells.
source: NCS1 failed to localize to the mother centriole without altering its cytoplasmic localization in CEP89 knockout cells but not in CEP15 knockout cells (Figure 2L and Figure 2—figure supplement 2B), indicating that CEP89 recruits NCS1 to the distal appendage.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2L and Figure 2—figure supplement 2B.

claim: The lack of NCS1 localization at the centriole in CEP89 knockout cells was rescued by expressing untagged CEP89.
source: The lack of NCS1 localization at the centriole in CEP89 knockouts cells was rescued by expressing untagged CEP89 (Figure 2L and Figure 2—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: The claim is supported by rescue experiment data shown in Figure 2L and Figure 2—figure supplement 2B.

claim: CEP15 localization requires CEP89 but not NCS1.
source: CEP15 localization required CEP89, but not NCS1 (Figure 2M and Figure 2—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2M and Figure 2—figure supplement 2C.

claim: Structural modeling using Alphafold2 shows that CEP89 interacts with both NCS1 and CEP15 whereas CEP15 does not interact with NCS1.
source: This is further corroborated by the structural modeling using Alphafold2, which shows that CEP89 interacts with both NCS1 and CEP15 whereas CEP15 does not interact with NCS1 (Figure 2O; Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by structural modeling data shown in Figure 2O and Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: The expression level of neither NCS1 nor CEP15 is affected by CEP89 depletion.
source: The expression level of neither NCS1 nor CEP15 was affected by CEP89 depletion (Figure 2—figure supplement 2D, E).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2D-E.

claim: Both NCS1 and CEP15 are recruited to the distal appendage by CEP89.
source: These results suggest that both NCS1 and CEP15 are recruited to the distal appendage by CEP89 (Figure 2N).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the localization dependency data.

claim: The localization of other distal appendage proteins is unchanged in cells deficient in CEP89, NCS1, or CEP15.
source: We also tested whether the three proteins affect localization of other distal appendage proteins and found that the localization of other distal appendage proteins were unchanged in cells deficient in CEP89, NCS1, or CEP15 (Figure 2—figure supplement 4A–C) (see also Figure 2A–L of Kanie et al., 2025).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 4A-C and referenced data.

claim: NCS1 localization is greatly diminished in CEP83 or SCLT1 knockouts.
source: Similar to the centriolar localization of CEP89, which was significantly reduced in CEP83 or SCLT1 knockouts, NCS1 localization was also greatly diminished in these knockouts (Figure 2—figure supplement 4D).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 4D.

claim: CEP83-SCLT1 module serves as a structural component of the distal appendage.
source: This is consistent with the observation that CEP83-SCLT1 module serves as a structural component of the distal appendage (see Kanie et al., 2025 for the detail).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to an accompanying paper.

claim: The feedback complex CEP164-TTBK2 is required for proper centriolar localization of NCS1.
source: In contrast, the feedback complex CEP164-TTBK2 (see Kanie et al., 2025 for the detail) was required for proper centriolar localization of NCS1 (Figure 2—figure supplement 4D) but not for CEP89 (Figure 2F of Kanie et al., 2025).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 4D and referenced data.

claim: The feedback complex CEP164-TTBK2 is not required for proper centriolar localization of CEP89.
source: In contrast, the feedback complex CEP164-TTBK2 (see Kanie et al., 2025 for the detail) was required for proper centriolar localization of NCS1 (Figure 2—figure supplement 4D) but not for CEP89 (Figure 2F of Kanie et al., 2025).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to data in an accompanying paper.

claim: CEP89 is a substrate of TTBK2.
source: Given that CEP89 is a substrate of TTBK2 (Bernatik et al., 2020; Lo et al., 2019), this might suggest that phosphorylation of TTBK2 could affect the interaction between CEP89 and NCS1.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Bernatik et al., 2020 and Lo et al., 2019.

claim: Phosphorylation by TTBK2 might affect the interaction between CEP89 and NCS1.
source: Given that CEP89 is a substrate of TTBK2 (Bernatik et al., 2020; Lo et al., 2019), this might suggest that phosphorylation of TTBK2 could affect the interaction between CEP89 and NCS1.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning based on the known phosphorylation relationship.

claim: NCS1 may be a phosphorylation target of TTBK2.
source: It is also possible that NCS1 may be a phosphorylation target of TTBK2.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning.

claim: Control RPE cells form cilia over 24 hr after serum starvation, and almost all cells complete cilium formation between 24 and 48 hr.
source: Control RPE cells form cilia over 24 hr after serum starvation, and almost of all cells completed cilium formation between 24 and 48 hr.
evidence: The claim is supported by kinetic analysis data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: CEP89 and NCS1 knockouts display a notable delay in initiating ciliation.
source: CEP89 and NCS1 knockouts displayed a notable delay in initiating ciliation (see 12 hr in Figure 3A), but gradually catch up on ciliogenesis and exhibited only mild ciliary formation defects at later time points (see 48 hr in Figure 3A).
evidence: The claim is supported by kinetic analysis data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: CEP89 and NCS1 knockouts gradually catch up on ciliogenesis and exhibit only mild ciliary formation defects at later time points.
source: CEP89 and NCS1 knockouts displayed a notable delay in initiating ciliation (see 12 hr in Figure 3A), but gradually catch up on ciliogenesis and exhibited only mild ciliary formation defects at later time points (see 48 hr in Figure 3A).
evidence: The claim is supported by kinetic analysis data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The cilium formation defect in CEP89 knockouts was rescued by expressing untagged CEP89.
source: The cilium formation defect was rescued by expressing untagged CEP89 in CEP89 knockouts or untagged NCS1 in NCS1 knockouts (Figure 3B).
evidence: The claim is supported by rescue experiment data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The cilium formation defect in NCS1 knockouts was rescued by expressing untagged NCS1.
source: The cilium formation defect was rescued by expressing untagged CEP89 in CEP89 knockouts or untagged NCS1 in NCS1 knockouts (Figure 3B).
evidence: The claim is supported by rescue experiment data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The kinetic defect in CEP89, NCS1, or CEP15 knockout cells is strongly consistent with the knockouts of several other distal appendage proteins, namely ANKRD26 and FBF1.
source: This kinetic defect is strongly consistent with the knockouts of several other distal appendage proteins, namely ANKRD26 and FBF1 (Figure 5A, B of Kanie et al., 2025).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to data in an accompanying paper.

claim: The ciliary length of CEP89, NCS1, or CEP15 knockout cells is comparable to that of control cells.
source: The ciliary length of CEP89, NCS1, or CEP15 knockout cells was comparable to that of control cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Ciliary ARL13B signal intensity is reduced in CEP89 or NCS1 knockouts even after the cells complete cilium formation.
source: Consistent with the cells deficient in ANKRD26 or FBF1 (see Figure 5—figure supplement 1 of Kanie et al., 2025), ciliary ARL13B signal intensity was reduced in CEP89 or NCS1 knockouts even after the cells complete cilium formation (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B–D).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B-D and citation.

claim: Even though NCS1 or CEP89 knockouts can eventually form primary cilia, those cilia may be functionally different from wild-type cilia.
source: This suggests that even though the NCS1 or CEP89 knockouts can eventually form primary cilia, those cilia may be functionally different from wild-type cilia.
evidence: This is inferred from the reduced ARL13B signal in cilia of knockout cells.

claim: CEP15 knockouts show similar but much milder kinetic defect of cilium formation than CEP89 or NCS1 knockouts.
source: CEP15 knockouts showed similar but much milder kinetic defect of cilium formation than CEP89 or NCS1 knockouts, therefore, we focused on NCS1 in the subsequent investigation.
evidence: The claim is supported by kinetic analysis data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: NCS1 knockouts exhibit moderate preciliary vesicle recruitment defect, similar to CEP89 knockouts, when assessed using RAB34 as the vesicle marker.
source: Indeed, NCS1 knockouts exhibited moderate preciliary vesicle recruitment defect, similar to CEP89 knockouts, when assessed using RAB34 as the vesicle marker (Figure 3C).
evidence: The claim is supported by vesicle recruitment assay data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Transmission electron microscopy analysis confirmed the vesicle recruitment defect in NCS1 knockouts.
source: Transmission electron microscopy analysis confirmed the vesicle recruitment defect in NCS1 knockouts (Figure 3D, E).
evidence: The claim is supported by electron microscopy data shown in Figure 3D-E.

claim: The presence of fused vesicles in NCS1 knockouts suggests that NCS1 is important for recruitment but not fusion of the vesicle.
source: The presence of fused vesicles, albeit much lower percentage than control cells, in NCS1 knockouts (Figure 3D, E) suggests that NCS1 is important for recruitment but not fusion of the vesicle.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation of fused vesicles in NCS1 knockout cells.

claim: Removal of CP110 is partially, but measurably affected in NCS1 knockout cells.
source: Removal of CP110, which is believed to act as a cap of axonemal microtubule, was partially, but measurably affected in NCS1 knockout cells (Figure 3F), consistent with the fact that CP110 removal is in part downstream of the vesicle recruitment (Figure 4D of Kanie et al., 2025).
evidence: The claim is supported by CP110 removal assay data shown in Figure 3F and citation.

claim: CP110 removal is in part downstream of the vesicle recruitment.
source: Removal of CP110, which is believed to act as a cap of axonemal microtubule, was partially, but measurably affected in NCS1 knockout cells (Figure 3F), consistent with the fact that CP110 removal is in part downstream of the vesicle recruitment (Figure 4D of Kanie et al., 2025).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to data in an accompanying paper.

claim: Neither IFT88 nor CEP19 recruitment to the centriole is affected in NCS1 knockout cells.
source: Neither IFT88 nor CEP19 recruitment to the centriole was affected in NCS1 knockout cells (Figure 3G, H).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 3G-H.

claim: NCS1 plays an important role in cilium formation by regulating preciliary vesicle recruitment, but not other known processes of cilium formation.
source: These results suggest that NCS1 plays an important role in cilium formation by regulating preciliary vesicle recruitment, but not other known processes of cilium formation, consistent with the role of CEP89 in preciliary vesicle recruitment.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental results showing specific defects in vesicle recruitment but not IFT/CEP19 recruitment.

claim: The distal appendage is indispensable for the recruitment of the preciliary vesicle to the mother centriole.
source: As we showed in an accompanying paper, the distal appendage is indispensable for the recruitment of the preciliary vesicle to the mother centriole.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to an accompanying paper.

claim: Virtually no RAB34-positive ciliary vesicle is observed at mother centriole in cells deficient in CEP164, CEP83, or TTBK2.
source: Virtually no RAB34-positive ciliary vesicle was observed at mother centriole in cells deficient in CEP164, CEP83, or TTBK2, which are critical for structural integrity of the distal appendage (Figure 5C of Kanie et al., 2025).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to data in an accompanying paper.

claim: CEP164, CEP83, and TTBK2 are critical for structural integrity of the distal appendage.
source: Virtually no RAB34-positive ciliary vesicle was observed at mother centriole in cells deficient in CEP164, CEP83, or TTBK2, which are critical for structural integrity of the distal appendage (Figure 5C of Kanie et al., 2025).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to data in an accompanying paper.

claim: The vesicle recruitment phenotype in CEP164, CEP83, or TTBK2 knockouts is much stronger than what was observed in CEP89 or NCS1 knockouts.
source: This phenotype is much stronger than what we observed in CEP89 or NCS1 knockouts (Figure 3C), suggesting that some other distal appendage proteins may compensate the lack of NCS1 for the preciliary vesicle recruitment.
evidence: The claim is inferred from comparing the severity of phenotypes.

claim: Some other distal appendage proteins may compensate for the lack of NCS1 in preciliary vesicle recruitment.
source: This phenotype is much stronger than what we observed in CEP89 or NCS1 knockouts (Figure 3C), suggesting that some other distal appendage proteins may compensate the lack of NCS1 for the preciliary vesicle recruitment.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning based on the partial phenotype in NCS1 knockouts.

claim: Depletion of NCS1 decreases the percentage of ciliated cells in each single knockout cell line (FBF1, ANKRD26, KIZ, LRRC45, INPP5E), except CEP89.
source: Cilium formation assay revealed that depletion of NCS1 decreased the percentage of ciliated cells in each single knockout cells, except CEP89 (Figure 4B, C).
evidence: The claim is supported by cilium formation assay data shown in Figure 4B-C.

claim: CEP89, but no other distal appendage protein, regulates the same ciliary formation pathway as NCS1.
source: This suggests that CEP89, but no other distal appendage protein regulates the same ciliary formation pathway as NCS1.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the double knockout data showing no additive effect for CEP89+NCS1 double knockout.

claim: Depletion of NCS1 decreases the RAB34-positive centriole in each of the single distal appendage knockout cells, except CEP89 knockouts.
source: Similarly, depletion of NCS1 decreased the RAB34-positive centriole in each of the single distal appendage knockout cells, except CEP89 knockouts (Figure 4D).
evidence: The claim is supported by vesicle recruitment assay data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Yet unknown distal appendage proteins are required to compensate for the preciliary vesicle recruitment defect of NCS1 knockout cells.
source: These results suggest that yet unknown distal appendage proteins would be required to compensate for the preciliary vesicle recruitment defect of NCS1 knockout cells.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning based on the partial phenotype and lack of complete epistasis with known proteins.

claim: One or more integral components (CEP164, TTBK2, SCLT1, and CEP83) may be directly involved in preciliary vesicle recruitment.
source: Another possibility is that one or more integral components (CEP164, TTBK2, SCLT1, and CEP83) may be directly involved in preciliary vesicle recruitment.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning.

claim: Myristoylation is required for membrane localization of NCS1.
source: In contrast, NCS1-G2A was only found in the soluble fraction (15,000 × g supernatant) (Figure 5A), suggesting that myristoylation is required for membrane localization of NCS1.
evidence: The claim is supported by subcellular fractionation data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Membrane localization of CEP89 requires NCS1 with an intact myristoylation motif.
source: Interestingly, CEP89 was only found in the soluble fraction (15,000 × g supernatant) in NCS1 knockout cells expressing either empty vector or NCS1-G2A, but not NCS1-WT. This suggests that membrane localization of CEP89 requires NCS1 with an intact myristoylation motif.
evidence: The claim is supported by subcellular fractionation data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Both wild-type and the myristoylation defective (G2A) NCS1 localize to the mother centriole to a similar extent when expressed at similar level to endogenous NCS1.
source: When expressed at similar level to endogenous NCS1 (Figure 5B), both wild-type and the myristoylation defective (G2A) NCS1 localizes to the mother centriole to a similar extent (Figure 5C, D).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 5C-D and expression data in Figure 5B.

claim: The myristoylation defective mutant of NCS1 almost completely fails to rescue ciliation defect of NCS1 knockout cells.
source: However, the myristoylation defective mutant almost completely failed to rescue ciliation and preciliary vesicle recruitment defect of NCS1 knockout cells (Figure 5E, F).
evidence: The claim is supported by rescue experiment data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: The myristoylation defective mutant of NCS1 almost completely fails to rescue preciliary vesicle recruitment defect of NCS1 knockout cells.
source: However, the myristoylation defective mutant almost completely failed to rescue ciliation and preciliary vesicle recruitment defect of NCS1 knockout cells (Figure 5E, F).
evidence: The claim is supported by rescue experiment data shown in Figure 5F.

claim: NCS1 recruits preciliary vesicle to the distal appendage via its myristoylation motif.
source: These data suggest that NCS1 recruits preciliary vesicle to the distal appendage via its myristoylation motif.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the rescue experiments showing myristoylation is required for function but not localization.

claim: The three intact Ca2+-binding EF hands and the Gly2 myristoylation site of NCS1 cluster on one face, while the CEP89-binding pocket occupies the opposite face.
source: Structural modeling of the NCS1–CEP89 complex reveals a distinct functional organization of NCS1 (Figure 5G). The three intact Ca2+-binding EF hands and the Gly2 myristoylation site cluster on one face of NCS1, while the CEP89-binding pocket occupies the opposite face.
evidence: The claim is supported by structural modeling data shown in Figure 5G.

claim: The arrangement of NCS1 functional domains suggests that NCS1 can simultaneously engage in membrane association and calcium sensing while interacting with CEP89.
source: This arrangement suggests that NCS1 can simultaneously engage in membrane association and calcium sensing while interacting with CEP89.
evidence: This is inferred from the structural model showing spatial separation of functional domains.

claim: Human NCS1 has three functional and one apparently non-functional EF-hand motif.
source: In addition to myristoylation motif, human NCS1 also has three functional and one apparently non-functional (due to the mutation in critical amino acids needed for co-ordination bond with calcium) EF-hand motifs (Bourne et al., 2001).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Bourne et al., 2001.

claim: Several other NCS family proteins, including Recoverin and Hippocalcin, show a calcium-myristoyl switch.
source: Several other NCS family proteins, including Recoverin and Hippocalcin, show a calcium-myristoyl switch (Ames et al., 1997; O'Callaghan et al., 2003).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Ames et al., 1997 and O'Callaghan et al., 2003.

claim: It has been proposed that NCS1 may employ a calcium-myristoyl switch similar to other NCS family proteins.
source: In this mechanism, the sequestered myristoylation motif is exposed to allow the protein to bind membrane upon calcium binding. It has been proposed that NCS1 may employ a similar molecular switch.
evidence: This is a statement about a hypothesis in the field.

claim: The structure of fission yeast Ncs1 solved by nuclear magnetic resonance spectroscopy showed the calcium-myristoyl switch.
source: While the structure of fission yeast Ncs1, solved by nuclear magnetic resonance spectroscopy showed the calcium-myristoyl switch (Lim et al., 2011), several lines of evidence suggest the absence of that type of switch in budding yeast and mammalian NCS1 (Ames et al., 2000; O'Callaghan et al., 2002; Lemire et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Lim et al., 2011.

claim: Several lines of evidence suggest the absence of calcium-myristoyl switch in budding yeast and mammalian NCS1.
source: While the structure of fission yeast Ncs1, solved by nuclear magnetic resonance spectroscopy showed the calcium-myristoyl switch (Lim et al., 2011), several lines of evidence suggest the absence of that type of switch in budding yeast and mammalian NCS1 (Ames et al., 2000; O'Callaghan et al., 2002; Lemire et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Ames et al., 2000; O'Callaghan et al., 2002; and Lemire et al., 2016.

claim: The E84Q mutant of NCS1 as well as any double and triple EF-hand mutants are highly destabilized.
source: The E84Q mutant as well as any double and triple EF-hand mutants were highly destabilized (see input in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A), and the centriolar NCS1 signal intensity of the mutants was reduced in parallel to their diminished expression level (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The first EF hand is indispensable for stability of NCS1.
source: This suggests that the first EF hand is indispensable for stability of NCS1.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the destabilization of E84Q mutant.

claim: The E120Q mutant of NCS1 has similar expression level to wild-type, but its centrosomal signal is significantly reduced.
source: E120Q mutant had similar expression level, but its centrosomal signal was significantly reduced (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B), consistent with its diminished interaction with CEP89 (see IP: GFP in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A), a protein that recruits NCS1 to the mother centriole (Figure 2L).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence and immunoblot data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A-B.

claim: The second EF hand is involved in keeping the structure of NCS1 to interact with CEP89.
source: This suggests that the second EF hand is involved in keeping its structure to interact with CEP89.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the reduced CEP89 binding of E120Q mutant.

claim: The E168Q mutation has a negligible effect on stability and localization of NCS1.
source: E168Q had a negligible effect in stability and localization of NCS1.
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A-B.

claim: None of single EF-hand mutants of NCS1 show significant cilium formation defect.
source: The ciliation assay revealed that none of single EF-hand mutants showed significant cilium formation defect (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C) despite the partial reduction of centriolar signal intensity for E84Q and E120Q.
evidence: The claim is supported by ciliation assay data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The double or triple EF-hand mutants of NCS1 almost completely fail to rescue ciliation defect of NCS1 knockout cells.
source: The double or triple mutants almost completely failed to rescue ciliation defect of NCS1 knockout cells (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C), reflecting their very low expression level (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by ciliation assay data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Calcium binding is primarily required for the structure and stability of NCS1.
source: These results suggest that calcium binding is primarily required for the structure and stability of NCS1 and NCS1 does not clearly exhibit a calcium-myristoylation switch.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the EF-hand mutant data.

claim: NCS1 does not clearly exhibit a calcium-myristoylation switch.
source: These results suggest that calcium binding is primarily required for the structure and stability of NCS1 and NCS1 does not clearly exhibit a calcium-myristoylation switch.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the EF-hand mutant data showing no clear switch mechanism.

claim: The structural role of calcium on NCS1 is largely consistent with NCS1's high binding affinity to calcium (~90 nM).
source: The structural role of calcium on NCS1 is largely consistent with NCS1's high binding affinity to calcium (−90 nM) (Aravind et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Aravind et al., 2008.

claim: Destabilization of microtubules by nocodazole immediately inhibits preciliary vesicle recruitment and subsequent cilium formation.
source: Consistent with the previous report (Wu et al., 2018), destabilization of microtubule by nocodazole (Figure 6A, B) immediately inhibited preciliary vesicle recruitment and subsequent cilium formation (Figure 6C, D), suggesting that preciliary vesicles are trafficked to the mother centriole via microtubules.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6C-D and citation to Wu et al., 2018.

claim: Preciliary vesicles are trafficked to the mother centriole via microtubules.
source: Consistent with the previous report (Wu et al., 2018), destabilization of microtubule by nocodazole (Figure 6A, B) immediately inhibited preciliary vesicle recruitment and subsequent cilium formation (Figure 6C, D), suggesting that preciliary vesicles are trafficked to the mother centriole via microtubules.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the nocodazole treatment data.

claim: Centriolar NCS1 signal gradually increases upon serum starvation even in the presence of nocodazole.
source: In contrast, centriolar NCS1 signal was gradually increased upon serum starvation even in the presence of nocodazole (Figure 6E), suggesting that NCS1 accumulates at the distal appendage by microtubule-independent mechanisms, possibly by diffusion, similar to the previously proposed diffusion-to-capture model of IFT trafficking to the ciliary base (Hibbard et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 6E.

claim: NCS1 accumulates at the distal appendage by microtubule-independent mechanisms, possibly by diffusion.
source: In contrast, centriolar NCS1 signal was gradually increased upon serum starvation even in the presence of nocodazole (Figure 6E), suggesting that NCS1 accumulates at the distal appendage by microtubule-independent mechanisms, possibly by diffusion, similar to the previously proposed diffusion-to-capture model of IFT trafficking to the ciliary base (Hibbard et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the nocodazole treatment data and citation to a similar model.

claim: NCS1 is unlikely to use the UNC119 pathway for trafficking to the distal appendage.
source: We conclude that NCS1 is unlikely to use the UNC119 pathway, as we did not observe UNC119A/UNC119B in our AP/MS analysis of CEP89 (Figure 1—source data 2), nor in purifications of UNC119A/UNC119B proteins themselves (Wright et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the absence of UNC119 in mass spectrometry data and citation.

claim: Centriolar NCS1 is comparable between control (sgSafe) and RAB34 knockout cells.
source: We confirmed that centriolar NCS1 was comparable between control (sgSafe) and RAB34 knockout cells (Figure 6F), suggesting that NCS1 is recruited to the centriole independently from the ciliary vesicle.
evidence: The claim is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 6F.

claim: NCS1 is recruited to the centriole independently from the ciliary vesicle.
source: We confirmed that centriolar NCS1 was comparable between control (sgSafe) and RAB34 knockout cells (Figure 6F), suggesting that NCS1 is recruited to the centriole independently from the ciliary vesicle.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the RAB34 knockout data.

claim: NCS1 moves to the distal appendage possibly by diffusion or an alternative trafficking mechanism and there it captures the preciliary vesicle that is trafficked to the centriole by microtubule-dependent trafficking.
source: These results suggest that NCS1 moves to the distal appendage possibly by diffusion or an alternative trafficking mechanism and there it captures the preciliary vesicle that is trafficked to the centriole by microtubule-dependent trafficking.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the combined nocodazole and RAB34 knockout data.

claim: NCS1 is expressed in a wide range of murine tissues.
source: We first tested the expression of NCS1 in various murine tissues and confirmed that NCS1 is expressed in a wide range of tissues (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1A.

claim: NCS1 localizes to both cytoplasm and the ciliary base in isolated hippocampal neurons.
source: When we performed immunofluorescence (IF) assay, NCS1 localized to both cytoplasm and the ciliary base (a dot next to ciliary markers, ARL13B or AC3) in isolated hippocampal neuron (top panel in Figure 7A) as well as cells in hypothalamus (Figure 7B) and the dentate gyrus of the hippocampus (Figure 7—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: NCS1 localizes to both cytoplasm and the ciliary base in cells in hypothalamus.
source: When we performed immunofluorescence (IF) assay, NCS1 localized to both cytoplasm and the ciliary base (a dot next to ciliary markers, ARL13B or AC3) in isolated hippocampal neuron (top panel in Figure 7A) as well as cells in hypothalamus (Figure 7B) and the dentate gyrus of the hippocampus (Figure 7—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: NCS1 localizes to both cytoplasm and the ciliary base in cells in the dentate gyrus of the hippocampus.
source: When we performed immunofluorescence (IF) assay, NCS1 localized to both cytoplasm and the ciliary base (a dot next to ciliary markers, ARL13B or AC3) in isolated hippocampal neuron (top panel in Figure 7A) as well as cells in hypothalamus (Figure 7B) and the dentate gyrus of the hippocampus (Figure 7—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 2C.

claim: Both cytoplasmic and centriole NCS1 signal is specific as no signal was detected in NCS1 knockout cells.
source: Both cytoplasmic and the centriole signal was specific for NCS1 as we detected no signal in NCS1 knockout cells (bottom panel in Figure 7A, B and Figure 7—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data comparing wild-type and knockout cells.

claim: NCS1 localizes to the ciliary base in virtually all non-neuronal ciliated cells tested, including kidney epithelia, pancreatic islet cells, airway epithelia, ependymal cells, and mouse embryonic fibroblasts (MEFs).
source: NCS1 also localized to the ciliary base in virtually all the non-neuronal ciliated cells that we tested, including kidney epithelia, pancreatic islet cells, airway epithelia, ependymal cells, and mouse embryonic fibroblasts (MEFs) (Figure 7C, D, Figure 7—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 7C-D and Figure 7—figure supplement 2A.

claim: NCS1 was not detected at the ciliary base in photoreceptor cells.
source: Only ciliated cells where we failed to detect NCS1 at the ciliary base were photoreceptor cells (Figure 7—figure supplement 2E).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 2E.

claim: Cilium formation is modestly perturbed in Ncs1-depleted MEFs.
source: In MEFs, cilium formation is modestly perturbed in Ncs1-depleted cells (Figure 7E), consistent with the kinetic cilium formation defect in RPE cells (Figure 3A).
evidence: The claim is supported by ciliation assay data shown in Figure 7E.

claim: Ciliary ARL13B signal is decreased in Ncs1−/− MEFs.
source: Decrease in ciliary ARL13B signal was also detected in Ncs1−/− MEFs (Figure 7F), similar to NCS1 knockout RPE cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B–D).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 7F.

claim: No measurable cilium formation defect was detected in hippocampal neurons that lack Ncs1.
source: In contrast, we did not detect a measurable cilium formation defect in hippocampal neurons that lack Ncs1 (Figure 7G), whereas the signal of ciliary membrane protein, type III adenylyl cyclase (ADCY3) (Bishop et al., 2007; Berbari et al., 2007), was significantly decreased (Figure 7H).
evidence: The claim is supported by ciliation assay data shown in Figure 7G.

claim: The signal of ciliary membrane protein ADCY3 is significantly decreased in Ncs1−/− hippocampal neurons.
source: In contrast, we did not detect a measurable cilium formation defect in hippocampal neurons that lack Ncs1 (Figure 7G), whereas the signal of ciliary membrane protein, type III adenylyl cyclase (ADCY3) (Bishop et al., 2007; Berbari et al., 2007), was significantly decreased (Figure 7H).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 7H and citations.

claim: Ncs1−/− mice do not exhibit preweaning lethality.
source: Inconsistent with the previous two reports (Nakamura et al., 2011; Dickinson et al., 2016), which generated Ncs1 knockout mice independently, our Ncs1−/− mice did not exhibit preweaning lethality (Figure 7A, p = 0.369 in Chi-square test in data with male and female combined).
evidence: The claim is supported by viability data shown in Figure 8A and citations to previous studies.
